The safety factor is the lowest eigenvalue, a load multiplier on the applied atmospheric pressure. Imperfections were not put into the finite-element model. They say a knockdown of 0.2 is recommended in their reference 20 for hemispherical sandwich domes, and that experimental knockdowns for homogeneous spherical shells often exceed 0.4. Intracell buckling gives R > 2.11 m. Adhesive mass is not included. Face wrinkling uses k2 = 0.82 and K = 0.95.

document.authors: Akhmeteli and Gavrilin

records.licence: CC BY 4.0.
records.quote: if R = 2.5 m, the mass of the shell is 75.7 kg, and the payload is 8.7 kg
records.confidence_reason: The example sentence, including 4.23 × 10^-5, 3.52 × 10^-3, 106 μm, 8.8 mm, 75.7 kg and 8.7 kg, was read from a page image of journal page 489. The 2.65 safety factor was read from the PDF text of the Figure 6 caption.
records.limits: A reproduction misses if, with these inputs and their air density, the shell mass is not 75.7 kg or the zero-buoyancy payload is not 8.7 kg. Their analytical thicknesses (3.9 × 10^-5 and 3.9 × 10^-3) are a different, earlier estimate. The finite-element text also says h3 ≈ 3.53 × 10^-3 at the eigenvalue peak; the discussion rounds the design to 3.52 × 10^-3. Use 3.52 × 10^-3 for the stated example. The body text points to Figure 7 for that 2.65 peak. A coarse 3D mesh gave a minimum eigenvalue of 3.0, which the authors say is subject to adjustment with a better mesh. This is a calculation, not a built balloon.
